A bottleneck cannot be solved by adding non-bottleneck equipment; map the process flow and constrained resource.

Northstar can make 8,075 units locally at contribution 120 per good unit or subcontract 2,000 additional units at incremental contribution 45 each. A local quality program raises yield from 95% to 98% at cost 50,000, increasing good units by 10,000×.85×(.98−.95)=255 and contribution 30,600, so it fails a one-year cash test without warranty savings or longer-term benefits. A second shift costing 80,000 adds 1,000 hours at the same 85% utilization and 95% yield, or ≈808 good units; contribution ≈96,900, preliminary gain ≈16,900, subject to demand and staffing.

For a global supplier, estimate joint exposure to exchange rates, tariffs, disruption and lead time. A cheap source may fail during an industry-wide shock simultaneously with demand peaks. Dual sourcing can buy option value beyond simple expected annual loss. Do not add probability-weighted losses from mutually overlapping events as if they were independent.

A Six Sigma-style improvement effort starts with a defined defect, measurement system and process capability, followed by root-cause tests and control plans. A defect-rate decline is meaningful only with comparable denominator and inspection intensity. Tie quality to returned units, warranty cash, customer losses and capacity recovery.
lessons.example: Effective output 10,000×.85×.95=8,075. Yield program adds 255×120=30,600 against 50,000. Second shift ≈807.5×120−80,000=16,900.
lessons.transfer: Stress yield to 90% and local contribution to 100; calculate good output and compare the second shift under those inputs.

lessons.title: Network flow and capacity choice under service commitments
body: A network optimization first defines nodes, arcs, capacities, demand and per-unit landed costs. A linear model minimizes ∑cost(i,j)×flow(i,j), subject to each plant’s output limit and every market’s demand. Do not optimize one route in isolation when the same scarce capacity serves multiple markets. Fixed site costs or all-or-nothing openings require integer variables.

Fictional Boreal has plants East cap80k and West cap60k; markets North demand70k and South demand50k, all figures in thousand units. Unit landed costs are East→North4, East→South6, West→North5, West→South3. Allocate West50 to South and East70 to North: cost150+280=430 thousand cost units, with spare East10 and West10. Moving x units of North from East to West adds x; moving x South from West to East adds 3x, so the displayed feasible solution is optimal under these simple costs and no additional arc limits. Document this exchange argument or solve the LP.

Suppose West loses30 capacity. Its available30 should serve South first at3 versus East6, while East must supply70 North and20 South, requiring90, above East cap80. The network is infeasible by10 without a third party or demand rationing; declaring a new cost from a spreadsheet without checking feasibility is wrong. An emergency supplier can provide South10 at9. Then East70 North and10 South cost280+60, West30 South costs90, and emergency10 South costs90, total520. Compare service penalties, timing and quality as well as money.

A resilience choice might prequalify emergency capacity for a fee. A 10% West outage probability with independent 30k capacity loss does not capture correlated storm effects at East or demand spikes. Use scenario trees with explicit joint events and a maximum acceptable service shortfall; capacity is an option in adverse states.
lessons.example: Normal cost430 in thousand unit×currency terms. West cap30 leaves 10k units infeasible without emergency supply; with emergency South10 at9, total280+60+90+90=520.
lessons.transfer: If emergency South cost12 instead of9, calculate the new stressed total; if North penalty is20 per short unit, compare a no-emergency rationing option.

lessons.title: Inventory pooling, service level and quality economics
body: Pooling uncertain demand can reduce safety stock if demand is not perfectly correlated. If two markets each have independent lead-time standard deviation100 units, separate 95% one-sided safety stock is1.65×100 each, total330. A centralized pool with equal service metric needs1.65×√(100²+100²)≈233, saving97 units. If demand correlation is .8, pooled standard deviation√(100²+100²+2×.8×100×100)≈189.7 and safety stock≈313, saving only17. The lead-time and service definitions must match.

At annual holding cost20/unit, independent pooling saving≈1,940/year; at correlation .8 it is≈340. A new hub costing10,000 annually cannot be justified by this safety-stock saving alone. It may still improve lead time, obsolescence or service, requiring a full network model. Pooling can also increase transportation cost and correlated outage exposure.

Quality is a cash-flow decision. Of100,000 units, a 2% defect rate creates2,000 defects. A process improvement costing90,000 reduces defect rate to.5%, avoiding1,500 defects. At warranty/rework cost80 per defect, gross annual saving120,000 and narrow net30,000. If inspection intensity changes, apparent defect trends may reflect measurement rather than production. Track failure modes and customer impact.

An executive should choose among inventory, capacity and quality methods according to the binding constraint, and test a joint case of high demand, supplier failure and defect escalation. Do not add overlapping lost-sales and warranty losses twice.
lessons.example: Independent safety stock330; pooled atρ0≈233, atρ.8≈313. Quality: (.02−.005)×100000×80−90000=30,000 net.
lessons.transfer: Set demand correlation to1 and defect cost50; recompute pooling and quality economics, then identify a nonnumeric constraint.

lessons.title: Least-cost distribution under capacity limits
body: A warehouse can ship 600 units at $4/unit; another can ship 500 at $7/unit. Demand is 900 units and both sites can serve it. The least-cost allocation fills the cheaper 600 and sends 300 from the second, for transport cost $4,500, assuming equal service and no fixed setup costs.
Decision practice: first reproduce the stated result, then identify missing evidence and explain why a different policy could dominate under a plausible counterfactual.
lessons.example: 600×4+300×7=4500; capacities and demand reconcile.
lessons.transfer: Change both the adverse probability or demand assumption and a material cost driver; show the revised calculation and a decision rule.

lessons.title: Economic order quantity and shortages
body: Annual demand is 20,000 units, fixed order cost $100, and annual holding cost $5 per unit. EOQ=sqrt(2×20,000×100/5)≈894 units. This assumes steady demand, instant replenishment and no stockouts or quantity discounts.
Decision practice: first reproduce the stated result, then identify missing evidence and explain why a different policy could dominate under a plausible counterfactual.
lessons.example: EOQ=sqrt(800000)=894.43 units.
lessons.transfer: Change both the adverse probability or demand assumption and a material cost driver; show the revised calculation and a decision rule.

lessons.title: Span of control and decision rights
body: A regional group with 48 teams reorganizes from 6 teams per manager to 8 teams per manager. Direct team-manager roles decline from 8 to 6, but the change can increase manager workload and require better coaching systems.
Board application: separate the numerical calculation from its strategic meaning. Explicitly state limitations, company data you would need, and at least one competing explanation.
lessons.example: 48/6=8 manager positions; 48/8=6, reduction 2.
lessons.transfer: Change two scenario inputs and explain the resulting downside and decision trade-off.

lessons.title: Pay incentives and unintended consequences
body: A sales bonus awards 5% of booked revenue on a $10M contract, or $500,000, despite a 20% gross margin. The award is 25% of the contract's $2M gross profit and may encourage low-margin growth.
Board application: separate the numerical calculation from its strategic meaning. Explicitly state limitations, company data you would need, and at least one competing explanation.
lessons.example: Bonus=.05×10M=.5M, gross profit=2M; bonus/GP=25%.
lessons.transfer: Change two scenario inputs and explain the resulting downside and decision trade-off.

lessons.title: Workforce retention economics
body: A 500-person critical workforce sees 18% annual turnover. Reducing it to 14% avoids 20 departures. At $35,000 replacement and ramp cost per departure, gross avoided cost=$700,000, before program costs.
Board application: separate the numerical calculation from its strategic meaning. Explicitly state limitations, company data you would need, and at least one competing explanation.
lessons.transfer: Change two scenario inputs and explain the resulting downside and decision trade-off.

lessons.title: Decision rights, coordination and organizational economics
body: Organizational structure assigns who can decide, who must be consulted and who is accountable for outcomes. A multinational can centralize purchasing to negotiate scale while decentralizing customer adaptation. The right design depends on information location, coordination cost and externalities. A matrix without clear tie-breaking rights can turn unresolved conflict into delayed decisions.

Fictional Helix employs 20 country teams. Central procurement offers 3% savings on a 200 million addressable spend, or 6 million, but an expected 2% service failure on 100 million contribution at risk would cost 2 million. A shared supplier data platform costs 1.5 million annually; simple net benefit is 2.5 million. If local compliance and customization raise service failure to 5%, expected loss is 5 million and net becomes −.5 million. These are scenario assumptions, not observed causal estimates.

Specify a governance contract: global sourcing owns standards and negotiated terms; country managers can exception on documented service or regulatory grounds; finance verifies realized savings and service losses. Incentives should include controllable cost, customer outcomes and a documented exception rate. Gross savings alone can reward a decision that destroys group value.

A diagnosis interviews cross-functional roles, maps decisions and queue times, then tests two explanations: unclear authority versus insufficient capacity. Run a limited pilot with a prespecified service metric and escalation window. Employee trust and lawful consultation are constraints, not residual terms in a spreadsheet.
lessons.transfer: If savings are 2% and service loss risk 3%, calculate net; propose an exception threshold that guards a country’s customer commitments.

lessons.title: Talent investment, incentives and ethical change
body: Executive talent decisions must measure capacity and retention without treating people as interchangeable inventory. A promotion pipeline can be evaluated using cohort transition rates, but adverse selection, manager incentives and unequal access to development need qualitative investigation. An apparent pay-performance correlation may reflect role selection or prior performance rather than causal incentive effects.

Helix proposes a manager program for 400 leaders at 4,000 each plus 400,000 implementation, total 2 million. If turnover among 4,000 critical staff falls from 16% to 14%, 80 fewer departures at 25,000 replacement and ramp cost each yield 2 million gross. The program just breaks even on this narrow annual measure, before productivity, employee benefit, and the risk that the change would have happened anyway.

Suppose a matched comparison group also sees turnover fall from 16% to 15%, while the treated group falls to 14%. A simple difference-in-differences estimate is a 1 percentage point extra reduction, not 2. Across 4,000 staff this represents 40 avoided departures and 1 million gross, leaving −1 million net under those assumptions. Parallel trends and spillover assumptions require investigation.

A change plan should define a baseline, explain the reason, involve affected staff, provide protected reporting channels and measure unintended effects such as burnout or gaming. A board should ask whether the proposed compensation system shifts risk onto workers or induces misleading reports. Separate ethical obligations from expected-value tradeoffs.
lessons.example: 400×4,000+400,000=2m cost. Raw avoided departures 4,000×.02=80, gross2m. Comparison-adjusted effect .01×4,000=40, gross1m; narrow net−1m.
lessons.transfer: At a replacement cost of 35,000, compute raw and comparison-adjusted annual net. Explain why neither proves a causal program effect.

lessons.title: Succession risk and organizational capacity
body: Succession planning identifies critical roles, ready-now coverage, development pathways and correlated departures. A nominal replacement chart is insufficient if one executive is listed for multiple critical roles or the same event removes several candidates. Assess decision rights and continuity of internal controls alongside cash cost.

Fictional Helix has six critical leadership positions. Four have independent ready-now successors and two rely on one shared candidate. A simple count reports6/6 coverage, but simultaneous vacancy in the two shared-candidate roles leaves one unfilled. If annual vacancy probabilities are10% for each of those two positions and independent, joint event probability is1%. If a common restructuring shock makes their vacancy events positively correlated,1% understates the joint tail. A specialist can model a joint probability directly rather than multiplying marginals.

A proposed leadership academy costs1.2 million now and improves continuity enough to avoid expected lost contribution .5 million at each of the next three year ends, discount10%. PV of savings=.5×2.48685≈1.243 million; narrow NPV≈.043 million. If the improvement lasts only two years, PV=.5×(1/1.1+1/1.1²)≈.868 million and NPV≈−.332 million. Neither calculation captures legal, ethical and safety obligations.

A board should request documented role coverage, time to competence, internal-mobility outcomes and independent evaluation. Avoid assuming executive pay or a training program caused observed turnover changes without a comparator. Assign ownership for succession, risk and confidential worker information.
lessons.example: Shared successor cannot cover two simultaneous vacancies. Academy three-year NPV≈.5×2.48685−1.2=.043m; two-year NPV≈−.332m.
lessons.transfer: If annual benefit is .4 rather than .5, compute three-year NPV; explain why expected value alone cannot decide duty of care.

lessons.title: Incentive-compatible restructuring and cultural risk
body: A restructuring has one-time severance and systems costs, recurring savings, lost capability and working-capital effects. Book charges can occur in a different period from cash payments. Respect employment consultation, notice and discrimination rules in the relevant jurisdictions; this lesson is not an assertion of current law. Model a no-action option as a real alternative.

Helix proposes a two-year consolidation: 8 million cash restructuring now, 6 million annual operating savings at each year end, but 1.5 million annual lost customer contribution from service disruption. At 10%, pretax NPV=−8+4.5×(1/1.1+1/1.1²)≈−.190 million. A staged option spends3 million now, achieves2.5 million net annual benefit for two years and retains the option to stop after year one; simple committed two-year NPV≈1.339 million. This ignores differential tax, salvage and later expansion, which require separate analysis.

If lost contribution is only .5 million annually, full consolidation net annual benefit5.5 and NPV≈1.545 million, overtaking the staged option on these narrow figures. The break-even loss for the full plan is 6−8/1.735537≈1.390 million annually. Make the choice contingent on a pilot measure of service loss, not an untested cultural assertion.

A compensation plan rewarding booked savings may encourage underreporting transition costs and harms. Use balanced scorecards with verified cash savings, customer retention, employee voice, safety and compliance. Document consultation, dignity and appeal mechanisms. The executive report should disclose who owns controls and which indicators halt the rollout.
lessons.example: Full plan NPV=−8+(6−1.5)×1.735537≈−.190m. Stage NPV=−3+2.5×1.735537≈1.339m. Break-even annual lost contribution≈1.390m.
lessons.transfer: At 12% discount and only1m lost contribution, recompute full and staged two-year NPVs, then describe a nonfinancial stop rule.

lessons.title: Project C — Corporate Restructuring and Risk decision laboratory
body: Helix Global has opening unrestricted cash40 million, forecast CFO12, required capex15 and debt maturity20 during the year. Without action closing cash is17, below a20 minimum. This is a liquidity timing issue even if accounting EBIT is positive. A lender may agree to extend10 of debt into next year for additional current-year cash interest. At a hypothetical6% incremental annual rate, interest cost .6 pretax, .45 after a25% tax assumption with usable deductions; no-action-plus-extension closes at26.55.

A full restructuring pays8 now, saves6 annual cash cost but loses1.5 annual customer contribution. First-year pretax improvement4.5 and after-tax improvement3.375 if deductions and profits are usable. With the same10 debt extension and .45 after-tax interest, cash closes at40−8+12+3.375−.45−15−10=21.925. A staged plan pays3 now and earns2.5 pretax annual net benefit, or1.875 after tax; with extension it closes25.425. Neither one-year cash number captures employee obligations, severance timing or later debt maturity.

On a two-year pretax basis at10% discount and ignoring debt refinancing, full restructuring NPV=−8+4.5×1.735537≈−.190; staged NPV=−3+2.5×1.735537≈1.339. If service loss is only .5 annually, full NPV rises to≈1.545. Contract termination penalties, consultation obligations, intellectual property and jurisdiction-specific employment rules require actual counsel review. A modeled expected cost cannot waive a duty.

Compare restructuring, staging and refinancing without mixing enterprise NPV with financing proceeds. Build a month-by-month cash floor, stakeholder impact register, measurable customer-service pilot, and stop criteria. Reference a real issuer’s MD&A and risk factors as context while keeping all Helix figures fictional.
lessons.example: No action cash17 below floor20. Extension only26.55 after .45 interest. Full plus extension21.925; staged plus extension25.425. Two-year full NPV−.190 vs stage+1.339.
lessons.transfer: If maturity is25 rather than20, compute all closing cash balances. State which option meets the20 floor and what financing or timing action is needed.

lessons.title: Attrition and intervention evaluation
body: A division of 800 employees has 16% turnover; a retention initiative projects 12% turnover at $900,000 annual cost. If each avoided departure saves $24,000, estimated avoided departures=32 and gross savings=$768,000, yielding a −$132,000 net direct annual effect before productivity and wellbeing effects.
Decision practice: first reproduce the stated result, then identify missing evidence and explain why a different policy could dominate under a plausible counterfactual.
lessons.transfer: Change both the adverse probability or demand assumption and a material cost driver; show the revised calculation and a decision rule.

lessons.title: Executive incentive risk and marginal rewards
body: A bonus plan awards 3% of revenue growth on an extra $20M sales, paying $600,000. If the new sales carry only 8% gross margin, gross profit is $1.6M and the bonus consumes 37.5% of incremental gross profit. Consider deferred cash collections and return on capital.
Decision practice: first reproduce the stated result, then identify missing evidence and explain why a different policy could dominate under a plausible counterfactual.
lessons.example: Bonus .6M; incremental GP 1.6M; bonus/GP 37.5%.
lessons.transfer: Change both the adverse probability or demand assumption and a material cost driver; show the revised calculation and a decision rule.

lessons.title: Contract exposure and remedies
body: A buyer forecasts a 6% late-delivery probability on $15M of goods, with a contractual liquidated damage amount equal to 10% of order value if applicable. Simplified expected damages exposure is $90,000, subject to enforceability and all contract terms.
Board application: separate the numerical calculation from its strategic meaning. Explicitly state limitations, company data you would need, and at least one competing explanation.
lessons.example: 15M×.10×.06=$90,000. Not a legal opinion.
lessons.transfer: Change two scenario inputs and explain the resulting downside and decision trade-off.

lessons.title: Corporate tax cash consequences
body: A fictional company with $40M taxable income and a hypothetical flat 25% tax rate has $10M estimated tax before credits, NOLs or timing differences. Book expense and cash taxes can differ.
Board application: separate the numerical calculation from its strategic meaning. Explicitly state limitations, company data you would need, and at least one competing explanation.
lessons.example: 40×.25=10M. Assumed rate is instructional, not a statement of applicable law.
lessons.transfer: Change two scenario inputs and explain the resulting downside and decision trade-off.

lessons.title: Compliance controls and expected costs
body: An illustrative control reduces incident probability from 8% to 3% on a $5M potential operational loss. Expected loss reduction is $250,000. A $180,000 annual control may be economical under simplistic risk neutrality, but regulation and duty matter beyond expected value.
Board application: separate the numerical calculation from its strategic meaning. Explicitly state limitations, company data you would need, and at least one competing explanation.
lessons.example: (.08−.03)×5M=.25M expected reduction; net .07M before other costs.
lessons.transfer: Change two scenario inputs and explain the resulting downside and decision trade-off.

lessons.title: Contract risk, intellectual property and competition controls
body: A multinational contract review identifies governing law, parties, performance obligations, payment, acceptance, remedies, limitation of liability, termination, dispute resolution and data/IP rights. A contract is not economically sound merely because forecast revenue exceeds variable cost. Legal enforceability and regulatory duties vary by jurisdiction; this exercise is education, not legal advice.

Fictional Ardent signs a 20 million supply contract with 12 million variable cost and 2 million implementation. Expected contribution before risk is 6 million. A 10% chance of a 5 million unrecovered breach loss gives illustrative expected loss .5 million, leaving 5.5 million; a 300,000 control that halves breach probability reduces expected loss .25 million and is not justified by this narrow expected-value measure alone. Duty, tail exposure, reputation and correlated losses can still favor it.

The board should map ownership of developed software, patents and trade secrets before agreeing to customer-funded customization. Confidentiality alone does not establish IP ownership. Competition concerns arise in exclusivity, information exchanges and coordination with competitors; substantive rules and enforcement vary across jurisdictions. A commercial manager must escalate potential antitrust issues rather than infer legality from a profit model.

For procurement and sales, keep a clause-by-clause risk register with counsel review and responsible owners. Test the counterparty’s insurance, creditworthiness and cyber controls. Do not assume a 10% liquidated-damages clause is automatically enforceable or caps every possible liability.
lessons.example: Pre-risk contribution 20−12−2=6m; expected breach loss .10×5=.5m, risk-adjusted 5.5m. Control reduces loss by (.10−.05)×5=.25m, less than .3m direct cost.
lessons.transfer: If breach severity is 8m and control cuts probability to 2%, recompute expected reduction and net benefit before legal obligations.

lessons.title: Tax timing, transfer pricing and compliance governance
body: Corporate tax analysis distinguishes statutory rates, effective tax expense, current taxable income and cash payment. Temporary book-tax differences can create deferred balances; they do not automatically change enterprise pretax cash flow. International structures add transfer pricing, withholding, indirect taxes, permanent establishment and treaty questions. Applicable law is jurisdiction and date specific; consult qualified counsel and tax professionals for actual transactions.

Ardent reports pretax book income 100 million. Assume depreciation for tax exceeds book by 20 million this year, no permanent differences and a hypothetical 25% tax rate. Taxable income is 80; current tax is 20. Total book tax expense is 25 under simplified deferred-tax accounting, so deferred tax expense is 5 and a deferred tax liability grows by 5. Net income is 75. Cash tax benefit is timing: later deductions will reverse under the assumptions.

If one country earns 40 million of the group pretax income and a different hypothetical rate applies, a simple weighted effective rate could differ, but it cannot be computed without allocations, credits and local rules. An internal transfer price may alter location of taxable income while leaving consolidated pretax profit unchanged, subject to arm’s-length documentation and audit risk. Board reports should show both after-tax cash timing and uncertain-tax-position exposure, not promise permanent savings from accelerated depreciation.

Build a compliance map for payroll, employment, VAT/sales tax, customs and reporting entities. Tax strategy also raises governance and reputational questions. An executive should document assumptions, dates, authorities and specialist signoff, then stress policy changes without claiming an educational case states live law.
lessons.example: Book pretax100; tax depreciation excess20; taxable80; current tax20 at hypothetical25%; total book tax expense25; deferred expense5; net income75.
lessons.transfer: If temporary excess depreciation is 12 rather than 20, compute current tax and deferred expense. Explain why net income under unchanged book pretax and tax rate remains 75.

lessons.title: Board controls, contract triggers and competing regulatory risks
body: A board-level risk register maps obligations, jurisdiction, counterparty, control owner, evidence and response threshold. Corporate law, employment protections, antitrust and data rules differ by location and date. This teaching scenario uses hypothetical contractual terms, not a legal conclusion. When conduct could restrict competition or affect worker rights, counsel should review the actual facts before implementation.

Fictional Cygnus has a 60 million annual distribution contract. A service failure carries a negotiated 2 million credit if valid and enforceable; modeled annual probability is8%. Simplified expected credit is.16 million. A 300,000 control reduces probability to2%, yielding .12 million expected-credit reduction, so expected contractual saving alone is below cost. But a failure could also destroy 5 million future contribution with conditional probability20%; expected retention loss before control is .08×.20×5=.08 million, after control .02×.20×5=.02 million. Joint saving .18 million still below .30 million under these assumptions. Duty, safety and extreme outcomes can override this narrow test.

An exclusivity clause might improve guaranteed volume but foreclose rivals; analyze actual market definition, share and local competition rules with specialists. IP ownership and confidentiality must be explicit for customer-funded software. A lawful control program includes independent reporting, retaliation protection, audit logs and escalation, not simply a low average penalty budget. An ethics review asks whether incentives reward suppression of incident reports.

For executive signoff, provide a clause matrix and a decision tree, showing the conditional probabilities without treating service credit and lost contribution as mutually exclusive. Keep legal enforceability and regulatory duty outside a simplistic expected-value answer.
lessons.example: Expected credit before=.08×2=.16m, after=.02×2=.04m; conditional retention loss before=.08×.2×5=.08m, after=.02×.2×5=.02m. Total saving=.18m vs control cost=.3m.
lessons.transfer: If service-credit severity rises to5m and retention loss is8m conditional at20%, recalculate savings; state which questions require counsel.

lessons.title: Deferred-tax reversals and international decision boundaries
body: A project’s taxes must distinguish book expense, taxable income and cash timing. Suppose Cygnus spends40 million on equipment now, with book depreciation10 million annually for four years; hypothetical tax depreciation is20, 12, 5 and3. At a 25% assumed rate and sufficient taxable profit, tax savings relative to book depreciation are2.5, .5, −1.25 and −1.75 million, summing zero before discounting. The deferred liability grows when tax depreciation exceeds book and reverses later.

At a 10% discount rate, the present value of the incremental tax-timing savings is2.5/1.1+.5/1.1²−1.25/1.1³−1.75/1.1⁴≈.550 million. Do not count these timing savings again if a project NPV already uses actual tax depreciation in cash taxes. If the company cannot use deductions immediately, cash benefit is deferred and PV falls.

A multinational may face withholding, indirect tax, customs, transfer-pricing and permanent-establishment questions beyond this example. Consolidated pretax group profit is not the same as taxable income in each jurisdiction. An internal transfer price reallocates divisional income but does not itself create group operating cash. Evaluate legal compliance, documentation and policy-change exposure before promising cross-border savings.

Compare two structures by after-tax cash and contractual risk, then record assumptions and decision rights. Obtain dated local law and specialist opinion for real action; do not infer current law from a hypothetical 25% rate.
lessons.example: Tax depreciation less book=10,2,−5,−7; tax timing cash=2.5,.5,−1.25,−1.75; undiscounted sum0; discounted PV≈.550m at10%.
lessons.transfer: If deductions cannot be used in year1 until year2, shift the first tax benefit one year and recalculate PV under a clearly stated carryforward assumption.

lessons.title: Choose the right method across seven corporate disciplines
body: The cumulative decision begins with a financial statement bridge, not an isolated ratio. Fictional Novus Group sells500 million, pays300 cost of sales and120 operating expense including20 depreciation, then10 interest. EBIT80; pretax70; at hypothetical25% tax, net income52.5. Receivables rise20, inventory10 and payables5, so CFO=52.5+20−20−10+5=47.5. Capex60 leaves CFO less capex−12.5. If opening cash20 and minimum cash15, closing cash7.5 without financing or changed investment, a7.5 shortfall. State debt maturities before declaring an expansion affordable.

Managerial analysis chooses a relevant-cost model for an internal bottleneck, ABC for tracing resource use, and discounted cash for investment. A setup pool600,000 over120 setups costs5,000 per setup; a custom product using80 setups and500 test-hours at200/hour receives500,000 assigned overhead. That allocation does not show whether the cost disappears if the product is dropped. A capital project costing10 now with6 at each of two year ends has NPV=−10+6/1.1+6/1.1²≈.413 at10%, before risk and capacity displacement.

Commercial evidence must separate test effect, forecast and collectable contract. Raising price100→110 with volume100,000→90,000 and variable cost60 changes contribution from4 to4.5 million; revenue falls from10 to9.9 million. Two opportunities,4 million at.6 and3 million at.3, have expected bookings3.3 million, not assured cash. At a bottleneck, product A contributes50 using2 hours versus B40 using1 hour; B yields40 per scarce hour versus A25. An EOQ with demand10,000, order cost200 and holding10 is√400,000≈632 units under the basic assumptions.

Workforce and governance constraints remain substantive. Reducing turnover among200 staff from15% to10% avoids ten departures under a causal assumption, worth.3 million at30,000 per replacement before program cost. Tax depreciation20 versus book10 at a hypothetical25% rate saves2.5 current cash tax relative to book timing if usable, but reverses later. A contractual credit of2 million with5% occurrence has simple expected cost.1 million, without resolving enforceability or duty. The final board choice requires a linked downside, independent written defense and specialist review where necessary.
lessons.example: Novus: EBIT80, NI52.5, CFO47.5, post-capex−12.5, cash floor gap7.5. Project NPV≈.413. Price change contribution4→4.5. Pipeline3.3; EOQ≈632; labor turnover saving .3; tax timing2.5.
lessons.transfer: Construct a recession case with price−5%, unit variable cost+5 on100,000 units, receivables+10 beyond base and a supplier interruption. Reconcile profit, CFO, liquidity and the investment decision without double-counting.

lessons.title: Jurisdictional profit mix and illustrative cash taxes
body: A fictional group earns taxable income of $40M in jurisdiction A at an assumed 25% tax rate and $20M in B at an assumed 15% rate. Before credits, cross-border adjustments, withholding and deferred taxes, illustrative aggregate current tax is $13M, an effective rate of 21.67% on $60M.
Decision practice: first reproduce the stated result, then identify missing evidence and explain why a different policy could dominate under a plausible counterfactual.
lessons.transfer: Change both the adverse probability or demand assumption and a material cost driver; show the revised calculation and a decision rule.

lessons.title: Compliance investment and tail risk
body: A compliance upgrade costs $300,000 annually and lowers an illustrative incident probability from 10% to 3% for a $5M loss. Expected loss reduction is $350,000; simple risk-neutral net expected benefit is $50,000, before regulatory obligations, severity uncertainty or correlated events.
Decision practice: first reproduce the stated result, then identify missing evidence and explain why a different policy could dominate under a plausible counterfactual.
lessons.example: (.10−.03)×5M−.3M=.05M net expected benefit.
lessons.transfer: Change both the adverse probability or demand assumption and a material cost driver; show the revised calculation and a decision rule.
